title: Group Theory — Detailed Reference
description: Group-theoretic vocabulary used throughout the multi-sheeted n-gon tiling project. Covers symmetry groups of tiles, fiber groups indexing sheets, and algebraic obstructions to flat-space tiling.

abelian-group.summary: A group whose operation is commutative: ab = ba for all elements a, b.
abelian-group.definition:
A group $(G, \cdot)$ with **commutative** operation: $ab = ba$ for all $a, b \in G$.

Examples: $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}_n$, $\mathbb{R}$ under addition.

Non-abelian examples relevant to the project: symmetric groups $S_n$ for $n \geq 3$, quaternion group, dihedral groups $D_n$ for $n \geq 3$, all rotation groups in 3D except $SO(2)$.

examples.title: Integers under addition
examples.body: $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ is abelian: $m + n = n + m$ for all integers $m, n$.

examples.title: Cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_n$
examples.body: The integers modulo $n$ under addition form an abelian group of order $n$.

examples.title: Non-abelian contrast
examples.body: The dihedral group $D_3$ (symmetries of an equilateral triangle) is non-abelian: a rotation followed by a reflection differs from the reflection followed by the rotation.

formulas.description: Commutativity condition defining an abelian group.

discrete-group.summary: A group equipped with the discrete topology, so that every element is isolated.
discrete-group.definition: A group with the **discrete topology**: all elements are isolated. Examples: $\mathbb{Z}$, the icosahedral group $I$, the modular group $PSL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

examples.title: Integers $\mathbb{Z}$
examples.body: The integers under addition form a discrete group: each integer $n$ is an isolated point in the discrete topology.

examples.title: Icosahedral group $I$
examples.body: The 60-element rotation group of the icosahedron is a finite (hence discrete) group.

examples.title: Modular group
examples.body: $PSL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ acts discretely on the upper half-plane and is a fundamental example in number theory and hyperbolic geometry.

finite-group.summary: A group with finitely many elements; appears as orientation groups, fiber groups, and rotation groups of Platonic solids in the tiling project.
finite-group.definition: A group with **finitely many elements**. Classification of finite simple groups is one of the great achievements of 20th-century mathematics. Finite groups appear as **orientation groups**, **fiber groups**, and **rotation groups of Platonic solids**.

examples.title: Cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_n$
examples.body: The cyclic group of order $n$ is the simplest finite group, generated by a single element.

examples.title: Symmetric group $S_n$
examples.body: $S_n$ has order $n!$ and is the largest finite group acting naturally on $n$ elements.

examples.title: Icosahedral group $I \cong A_5$
examples.body: The rotation group of the icosahedron has order 60 and is the smallest non-abelian simple group.

cyclic-group.summary: The group of order n generated by a single element; realized as integers mod n or as n-th roots of unity.
cyclic-group.definition:
The group of order $n$ generated by **one element**: $\mathbb{Z}_n = \langle g \mid g^n = 1 \rangle$. Realized as **integers modulo $n$** under addition, or as **$n$-th roots of unity** under multiplication.

In the project: $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ is the orientation group of the pentagon expansion family (10 rotational copies of the tile).

examples.title: $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ as orientation group
examples.body: The pentagon expansion family has 10 rotational copies of each tile. The orientation group is $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$, generated by a $36°$ rotation, since the angular deficit of a pentagonal vertex is $36° = 360°/10$.

examples.title: Roots of unity
examples.body: The $n$-th roots of unity $\{e^{2\pi i k/n} : k = 0, \ldots, n-1\}$ under multiplication form a cyclic group isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_n$.

formulas.description: Presentation of the cyclic group of order n by a single generator g of order n.

dihedral-group.summary: The symmetry group of the regular n-gon, of order 2n, generated by a rotation and a reflection.
dihedral-group.definition:
The **symmetry group of the regular $n$-gon**, of order $2n$. Generated by a rotation $r$ of order $n$ and a reflection $s$ of order 2 with relation $srs = r^{-1}$.

Presentation: $D_n = \langle r, s \mid r^n = s^2 = (rs)^2 = 1 \rangle$.

examples.title: $D_3$ — symmetries of the equilateral triangle
examples.body: $D_3$ has order 6: three rotations ($0°$, $120°$, $240°$) and three reflections. It is isomorphic to $S_3$.

examples.title: $D_5$ — symmetries of the regular pentagon
examples.body: $D_5$ has order 10: five rotations (multiples of $72°$) and five reflections. The rotation subgroup is $C_5 \cong \mathbb{Z}_5$.

formulas.description: Group presentation of the dihedral group of order 2n.

variables.n: number of sides of the polygon

klein-four-group.summary: The group Z_2 × Z_2 of order 4; abelian, with every non-identity element of order 2; the smallest non-cyclic group.
klein-four-group.definition: The group $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$, **order 4**, abelian, every non-identity element has order 2. Smallest non-cyclic group.

examples.title: Symmetries of a rectangle
examples.body: The symmetry group of a non-square rectangle (identity, horizontal reflection, vertical reflection, 180° rotation) is isomorphic to the Klein four-group.

formulas.expression: V_4 = \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 = \{e, a, b, ab\},\quad a^2 = b^2 = (ab)^2 = e
formulas.description: Structure of the Klein four-group: every non-identity element squares to the identity.

symmetric-group.summary: The group of all permutations of n elements, of order n!; non-abelian for n ≥ 3.
symmetric-group.definition: The group of **all permutations** of $n$ elements. Order $n!$. Non-abelian for $n \geq 3$.

examples.title: $S_3$ — permutations of 3 elements
examples.body: $S_3$ has order $3! = 6$ and is the smallest non-abelian group. It is isomorphic to $D_3$.

examples.title: $S_4 \cong O$ (octahedral group)
examples.body: The rotation group of the cube is isomorphic to $S_4$, the symmetric group on 4 elements (corresponding to the 4 main diagonals of the cube).

formulas.description: The order of the symmetric group on n elements.

alternating-group.summary: The group of even permutations of n elements; a subgroup of S_n of index 2 and order n!/2; simple for n ≥ 5.
alternating-group.definition:
The group of **even permutations** of $n$ elements. Subgroup of $S_n$ of index 2, hence order $n!/2$. Simple for $n \geq 5$.

Importance: $A_5 \cong I$ (icosahedral rotation group).

examples.title: $A_5 \cong I$
examples.body: The alternating group on 5 elements is isomorphic to the icosahedral rotation group $I$. It has order 60 and is the smallest non-abelian simple group.

examples.title: $A_4 \cong T$
examples.body: The alternating group on 4 elements is isomorphic to the tetrahedral rotation group $T$, of order 12.

formulas.description: The order of the alternating group on n elements.

quaternion-group.summary: The order-8 group {±1, ±i, ±j, ±k} defined by i²=j²=k²=ijk=−1; foundational for spin physics and the binary icosahedral group.
quaternion-group.definition:
The group $Q_8 = \{\pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$ of **order 8**. Defined by:

$$i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1$$

Non-abelian, smallest non-trivial double cover. Foundational for spin physics and the binary icosahedral group.

examples.title: Unit quaternions
examples.body: The eight elements $\{\pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$ under quaternion multiplication form $Q_8$. The element $-1$ is central and has order 2; $i, j, k$ each have order 4.

examples.title: Double cover structure
examples.body: $Q_8$ is a double cover of the Klein four-group $V_4$: the quotient $Q_8 / \{\pm 1\} \cong V_4$.

formulas.description: Defining relations of the quaternion group $Q_8$.

orthogonal-group.summary: The group of distance-preserving linear maps of R^n; n×n matrices satisfying A^T A = I, with two components (rotations and reflections).
orthogonal-group.definition: The group of **distance-preserving linear maps** of $\mathbb{R}^n$, equivalently $n \times n$ matrices with $A^T A = I$. Has two components: determinant $+1$ (rotations) and $-1$ (reflections).

examples.title: $O(2)$ — planar isometries fixing the origin
examples.body: $O(2)$ consists of rotations (by any angle) and reflections in lines through the origin. The rotation subgroup is $SO(2) \cong S^1$.

examples.title: $O(3)$ — spatial isometries fixing the origin
examples.body: $O(3)$ includes all rotations and improper rotations (reflections, inversions) in 3D space.

formulas.expression: O(n) = \{ A \in M_{n\times n}(\mathbb{R}) \mid A^T A = I \}
formulas.description: Definition of the orthogonal group as matrices whose transpose equals their inverse.

rotation-group-son.summary: The special orthogonal group of orientation-preserving isometries of R^n; matrices with A^T A = I and det A = +1.
rotation-group-son.definition: The **special orthogonal group** — orientation-preserving subgroup of $O(n)$, consisting of matrices with **determinant $+1$**. The identity component of $O(n)$.

examples.title: $SO(2)$ — planar rotations
examples.body: $SO(2)$ consists of all rotations of the plane about the origin. It is isomorphic to the circle group $S^1$.

examples.title: $SO(3)$ — spatial rotations
examples.body: $SO(3)$ is the group of all rotations of 3D space. Its finite subgroups are classified: cyclic, dihedral, tetrahedral, octahedral, and icosahedral.

formulas.description: The special orthogonal group as the orientation-preserving subgroup of O(n).

rotation-group-so3-subgroups.summary: Complete classification of finite subgroups of SO(3): cyclic C_n, dihedral D_n, tetrahedral T≅A_4, octahedral O≅S_4, and icosahedral I≅A_5.
rotation-group-so3-subgroups.definition:
The finite subgroups of $SO(3)$ are classified:

- **Cyclic** $C_n$: rotation by $2\pi/n$ about an axis.
- **Dihedral** $D_n$: $C_n$ together with $n$ perpendicular half-turns.
- **Tetrahedral** $T \cong A_4$: order 12.
- **Octahedral** $O \cong S_4$: order 24.
- **Icosahedral** $I \cong A_5$: order 60.

Plus **reflection extensions** in $O(3)$: adding inversions or reflections.

This classification limits which orientation groups can occur in flat-space tilings.

examples.title: Pentagon tiling orientation group
examples.body: The orientation group of the pentagon expansion family is $C_{10} \cong \mathbb{Z}_{10}$, a cyclic subgroup of $SO(2) \subset SO(3)$.

examples.title: Icosahedral tiling
examples.body: For $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$-tilings, the relevant orientation group is $I \cong A_5$, the icosahedral subgroup of $SO(3)$.

tetrahedral-group.summary: The rotation group of the regular tetrahedron, isomorphic to A_4, of order 12.
tetrahedral-group.definition: The **rotation group of the regular tetrahedron**, isomorphic to $A_4$, order 12. Generated by 8 face rotations and 3 edge rotations (plus identity).

examples.title: Rotations of the tetrahedron
examples.body: The 12 rotations of the tetrahedron consist of: the identity, 8 rotations by $120°$ and $240°$ about axes through vertices and opposite face centers, and 3 rotations by $180°$ about axes through midpoints of opposite edges.

formulas.description: The tetrahedral rotation group is isomorphic to the alternating group on 4 elements and has order 12.

octahedral-group.summary: The rotation group of the cube/octahedron, isomorphic to S_4, of order 24.
octahedral-group.definition: The **rotation group of the cube/octahedron**, isomorphic to $S_4$, order 24.

examples.title: Cube diagonals
examples.body: The 24 rotations of the cube permute its 4 main diagonals, giving an isomorphism $O \cong S_4$.

formulas.description: The octahedral rotation group is isomorphic to the symmetric group on 4 elements and has order 24.

icosahedral-group.summary: The rotation group of the icosahedron/dodecahedron, isomorphic to A_5, of order 60; a simple group playing the role for Q(√5)-tilings that S_4 plays for Z-tilings.
icosahedral-group.definition: The **rotation group of the icosahedron/dodecahedron**, isomorphic to $A_5$, order 60. A simple group — one of the smallest non-abelian simple groups. Plays the same role for $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$-tilings that $S_4$ plays for $\mathbb{Z}$-tilings.

examples.title: Simplicity of $A_5$
examples.body: $A_5 \cong I$ is simple: it has no proper normal subgroups. This is why the general quintic polynomial is not solvable by radicals.

examples.title: Role in pentagonal tilings
examples.body: For multi-sheeted pentagonal tilings over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$, the icosahedral group $I$ governs the orientation structure, analogously to how $S_4$ governs cubic tilings.

formulas.description: The icosahedral rotation group is isomorphic to the alternating group on 5 elements and has order 60.

spin-group.summary: The double cover of SO(n); has the same Lie algebra as SO(n) but requires a 4π rotation to return to the identity.
spin-group.definition: The **double cover of $SO(n)$**. Algebraically, $\text{Spin}(n)$ has the same Lie algebra as $SO(n)$ but a "twisted" topology where the loop $2\pi$-rotation generator becomes **non-trivial** (it takes a $4\pi$ rotation to return to identity in $\text{Spin}(n)$).

examples.title: $\text{Spin}(3) \cong SU(2)$
examples.body: The spin group in 3D is isomorphic to $SU(2)$, the group of unit quaternions. The covering map $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ sends each unit quaternion $q$ to the rotation $v \mapsto qv\bar{q}$.

examples.title: Spinor doubling
examples.body: A spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ particle's wave function transforms under $SU(2)$ representations that are not representations of $SO(3)$: a $2\pi$ rotation sends the state to its negative.

formulas.description: The fundamental group of SO(n) is Z_2 for n≥3, so Spin(n) is the unique simply-connected double cover.

su2-to-so3.summary: The canonical double cover of SO(3) by SU(2); encodes spinor doubling where spin-½ wave functions require a 4π rotation to return to their original state.
su2-to-so3.definition:
The **canonical double cover** in 3D. $SU(2)$ is the group of $2 \times 2$ unitary matrices with determinant 1, isomorphic to the unit quaternions. The map sends each unit quaternion $q$ to the rotation $v \mapsto q v \bar{q}$.

Encodes **spinor doubling**: spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ wave functions live in representations of $SU(2)$ that are not representations of $SO(3)$.

examples.title: Kernel of the covering map
examples.body: The kernel of $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ is $\{+I, -I\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$. Both $q$ and $-q$ represent the same rotation, but differ as spinor states.

examples.title: Spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ particle
examples.body: Under a $2\pi$ rotation, a spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ wave function acquires a factor of $-1$. Only after a $4\pi$ rotation does it return to its original value.

formulas.description: The covering homomorphism from SU(2) to SO(3) via quaternion conjugation.

variables.v: pure imaginary quaternion representing a vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$

aliases: double cover of a finite rotation group
binary-group.summary: The preimage in SU(2) of a finite rotation subgroup of SO(3); has twice the order of the original group.
binary-group.definition:
The **double cover in $SU(2)$** of a finite rotation group in $SO(3)$. For each finite subgroup $H \subset SO(3)$, the binary group $\tilde H = \pi^{-1}(H)$ in $SU(2)$ has order $2|H|$.

Examples:

- Binary tetrahedral $2T$, order 24.
- Binary octahedral $2O$, order 48.
- Binary icosahedral $2I$, order 120.

examples.title: Binary tetrahedral group $2T$
examples.body: The preimage of the tetrahedral group $T \cong A_4$ (order 12) in $SU(2)$ is the binary tetrahedral group $2T$ of order 24.

examples.title: Binary octahedral group $2O$
examples.body: The preimage of the octahedral group $O \cong S_4$ (order 24) in $SU(2)$ is the binary octahedral group $2O$ of order 48.

examples.title: Binary icosahedral group $2I$
examples.body: The preimage of the icosahedral group $I \cong A_5$ (order 60) in $SU(2)$ is the binary icosahedral group $2I$ of order 120, also known as the 120 icosian quaternions.

formulas.description: The binary group is the full preimage of a finite rotation group H under the covering map π: SU(2) → SO(3).

binary-icosahedral-group.summary: The order-120 double cover of the icosahedral group I in SU(2); equivalent to the 120 icosian quaternions and the vertex set of the 600-cell; encodes spinor-like holonomy of pentagonal multi-sheeted covers.
binary-icosahedral-group.definition:
**Order-120 double cover** of $I$ in $SU(2)$. Equivalently, the **120 icosian quaternions**. Equivalently, the vertex set of the 600-cell.

Importance: encodes the **spinor-like holonomy** of pentagonal multi-sheeted covers.

examples.title: 600-cell vertices
examples.body: The 120 vertices of the 600-cell (a regular 4-polytope) form the binary icosahedral group $2I$ under quaternion multiplication.

examples.title: Spinor holonomy
examples.body: In the pentagonal multi-sheeted cover, traversing a loop around a vortex accumulates a monodromy element in $2I$, reflecting the spinor-like $4\pi$-rotation symmetry.

formulas.description: The binary icosahedral group as the preimage of the icosahedral group under the SU(2)→SO(3) covering map.

lift.summary: An element of a covering group mapping to a given group element; in a double cover, each element has exactly two lifts.
lift.definition: An **element of a covering group mapping to a given group element**. In a double cover $\tilde G \to G$, each $g \in G$ has exactly two lifts $\pm \tilde g \in \tilde G$.

examples.title: Lifts in $SU(2) \to SO(3)$
examples.body: Each rotation $R \in SO(3)$ has exactly two lifts $\pm q \in SU(2)$, where $q$ is a unit quaternion with $\phi(q) = R$. The two lifts differ by the central element $-1 \in SU(2)$.

formulas.description: In a double cover, each element g has exactly two lifts, related by the non-trivial deck transformation.

variables.\\tilde{g}: one lift in the covering group $\tilde{G}$

reflection-group.summary: A group generated by reflections in hyperplanes; includes finite Coxeter groups, symmetry groups of Platonic solids, and wallpaper/crystallographic groups.
reflection-group.definition:
A group generated by **reflections** in hyperplanes. Includes:

- Finite reflection groups (Coxeter groups of finite type).
- Symmetry groups of Platonic solids (with reflections included).
- Wallpaper and crystallographic groups.

examples.title: Dihedral group $D_n$ as a reflection group
examples.body: $D_n$ is generated by two reflections in lines meeting at angle $\pi/n$. The product of these two reflections is a rotation by $2\pi/n$.

examples.title: Coxeter group of type $A_2$
examples.body: The Coxeter group $A_2$ is generated by two reflections $s_1, s_2$ with $(s_1 s_2)^3 = 1$, giving the dihedral group $D_3 \cong S_3$ of order 6.

wallpaper-group.summary: One of the 17 crystallographic groups of R² governing periodic planar patterns; notably excludes 5-fold rotational symmetry.
wallpaper-group.definition: One of the **17 crystallographic groups of $\mathbb{R}^2$** — the 17 inequivalent symmetry groups of periodic planar patterns. These are precisely the groups containing two linearly independent translations. The pentagon is excluded from this list: no wallpaper group has 5-fold rotational symmetry.

examples.title: Square lattice symmetry
examples.body: The symmetry group of the square lattice is the wallpaper group $p4m$, containing 4-fold rotations, reflections, and glide reflections.

examples.title: Pentagon exclusion
examples.body: No wallpaper group contains a 5-fold rotation. This is the crystallographic restriction theorem: only 2-, 3-, 4-, and 6-fold rotations are compatible with a periodic lattice in 2D.

permutation-group.summary: A group acting by permutations of a set; by Cayley's theorem, every group is a permutation group.
permutation-group.definition: A group acting by **permutations of a set**. Every group is a permutation group (Cayley's theorem), and every finite group embeds into some $S_n$.

examples.title: Cayley's theorem
examples.body: Every group $G$ of order $n$ embeds into $S_n$ via the left regular representation: $g \mapsto (h \mapsto gh)$.

examples.title: Symmetry group as permutation group
examples.body: The symmetry group of a regular polygon acts by permuting its vertices, giving an embedding into $S_n$ where $n$ is the number of vertices.

fiber-group.summary: The group indexing sheets in a covering space or principal G-bundle; for pentagons, G = Z_10 since the 36° deficit is 360°/10.
fiber-group.definition: The **group indexing sheets** in a covering space or principal $G$-bundle. Tiles on different sheets are related by $G$-action. For pentagons in the project: $G = \mathbb{Z}_{10}$ (cyclic of order 10, since the deficit $36° = 360°/10$ is the smallest rotation absorbing pentagonal frustration).

examples.title: $G = \mathbb{Z}_{10}$ for pentagons
examples.body: The angular deficit at each pentagonal vertex is $36°$. The fiber group $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ tracks which of the 10 rotational sheets a tile belongs to, with sheet transitions accumulating this deficit.

examples.title: Binary icosahedral fiber group
examples.body: In 3D pentagonal tilings, the fiber group may be the binary icosahedral group $2I$ of order 120, encoding spinor-like holonomy.

principal-g-bundle.summary: A fiber bundle whose fibers are copies of a group G with G acting by right multiplication; discrete principal G-bundles model multi-sheeted covers via G-valued edge transitions.
principal-g-bundle.definition:
A **fiber bundle whose fibers are copies of group $G$** equipped with $G$-action by right multiplication. Local trivializations:

$$\pi^{-1}(U) \cong U \times G$$

with transition functions valued in $G$. **Discrete principal $G$-bundles** model the multi-sheeted covers in the project: each edge crossing yields a $G$-element (the sheet transition).

examples.title: Multi-sheeted pentagon cover
examples.body: The 10-sheeted cover of the pentagonal tiling is a discrete principal $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$-bundle over the adjacency graph. Each edge crossing between tiles contributes a $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$-valued transition.

examples.title: Frame bundle
examples.body: The frame bundle of a Riemannian manifold is a principal $O(n)$-bundle whose sections are orthonormal frames.

formulas.description: Local trivialization of a principal G-bundle over an open set U.

variables.U: open subset of the base space

cayley-graph.summary: A graph encoding group structure with vertices as group elements and edges connecting g to gs for each generator s; G acts on it by left multiplication.
cayley-graph.definition:
A **graph encoding the group structure**:

- **Vertices**: group elements.
- **Edges**: between $g$ and $gs$ for each generator $s$ in a chosen generating set.

Properties:

- $G$ acts on its Cayley graph by left multiplication (graph automorphisms).
- Different generating sets give different Cayley graphs (but with the same underlying group).
- Useful for **visualizing finite groups** and computing geodesic word lengths.

examples.title: Cayley graph of $\mathbb{Z}_n$
examples.body: With generator $\{1\}$, the Cayley graph of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a cycle of length $n$.

examples.title: Cayley graph of $D_3$
examples.body: With generators $\{r, s\}$ (rotation and reflection), the Cayley graph of $D_3$ is a hexagonal prism graph, reflecting the 6 elements and their generator relationships.

holonomy-group.summary: The group of monodromies around all loops in a bundle; for a discrete principal G-bundle, it is the subgroup of G generated by all loop monodromies.
holonomy-group.definition: The **group of monodromies around loops** in a bundle. For a discrete principal $G$-bundle, the holonomy group is a subgroup of $G$ generated by all loop monodromies.

examples.title: Holonomy of the pentagonal cover
examples.body: For the 10-sheeted pentagonal cover, the holonomy group is a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ generated by the $36°$ monodromy of vortex-encircling loops.

examples.title: Flat connection
examples.body: A discrete principal $G$-bundle has trivial holonomy group (holonomy $= \{e\}$) if and only if the connection is flat — all loop monodromies are trivial.

monodromy.summary: The holonomy of a single closed loop — a fiber group element obtained by accumulating sheet transitions; for the pentagon cover, equals the 36° deficit angle.
monodromy.definition: The **holonomy of a single closed loop** — an element of the fiber group obtained by accumulating sheet transitions along the loop. For the pentagon's multi-sheeted cover, the monodromy of a vortex-encircling loop equals the deficit angle, $36°$.

examples.title: Pentagon vortex monodromy
examples.body: Traversing a loop that encircles a single pentagonal vertex accumulates a sheet transition of $36° = 1 \in \mathbb{Z}_{10}$, the generator of the fiber group.

examples.title: Trivial monodromy
examples.body: A loop that does not encircle any vortex has trivial monodromy (the identity element of $G$), returning to the same sheet.

formulas.description: The monodromy of a loop γ is the product of the G-valued edge transitions along the loop.

variables.\\gamma: a closed loop in the base space

braid-group.summary: The group of braids on n strands, generated by elementary strand-swaps σ_i; underlies anyonic statistics in 2D quantum systems and the Yang–Baxter equation.
braid-group.definition:
The **group of braids on $n$ strands**, denoted $B_n$. Generated by $n-1$ elementary braids $\sigma_i$ (swap of adjacent strands), with relations:

$$\sigma_i \sigma_j = \sigma_j \sigma_i \quad (|i - j| \geq 2)$$
$$\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1}$$

The second is the **braid relation**, central to the Yang–Baxter equation.

Importance:

- Underlies **anyonic statistics** in 2D quantum systems.
- Quotient by $\sigma_i^2 = 1$ gives the symmetric group $S_n$ (bosons/fermions).
- Mapping class group of the $n$-punctured disk equals $B_n$.

examples.title: Quotient to $S_n$
examples.body: Adding the relation $\sigma_i^2 = 1$ to the braid group $B_n$ gives the symmetric group $S_n$. This corresponds to passing from anyonic statistics (where exchanging particles twice need not be trivial) to bosonic/fermionic statistics.

examples.title: Mapping class group
examples.body: The mapping class group of the disk with $n$ punctures is isomorphic to $B_n$. Each generator $\sigma_i$ corresponds to a Dehn twist around a curve separating the $i$-th and $(i+1)$-th punctures.

formulas.description: The braid relation (Yang–Baxter equation in the braid group), relating adjacent generators.
Far-commutativity: non-adjacent elementary braids commute.

variables.\\sigma_i, \\sigma_j: elementary braids on non-adjacent strand pairs
